questions.q: Based on verified Anthropic pricing in this lesson, which tier is both the cheapest and fastest?
options: Claude Fable 5.1
Claude Opus 5.5
Claude Haiku 4.5
Claude Sonnet 5.5
questions.explain: Claude Haiku 4.5 is priced at $1/$5 per million tokens and described as the fastest tier — cheaper and faster than Sonnet, Opus, or Fable.

questions.q: What does self-attention compute for each token?
options: A weighted relevance score against every other token in the sequence
A spell-check correction for that token
The token's exact dictionary definition
A random number used only for training
questions.explain: Self-attention produces, for every token, a learned weight describing how relevant each other token is to it — regardless of distance.

questions.q: Which condition from the lesson increases the likelihood of hallucination?
options: Asking a precise question about a well-documented, widely discussed topic
Using a very short prompt with no follow-up questions
Asking for a precise citation or statistic on a topic the model has thin training coverage of
Asking the model to repeat a sentence verbatim
questions.explain: Specificity without grounding — like an exact citation on a niche topic — pushes the model to generate from a general pattern rather than a memorized fact, increasing hallucination risk.

questions.q: What is an embedding?
options: A vector (list of numbers) that represents a token's or text's meaning
A compressed version of the original text's characters
A password used to access the model's API
The literal dictionary definition stored as text
questions.explain: An embedding is a learned vector of numbers — hundreds to thousands of dimensions — that represents meaning, not a text compression or a dictionary lookup.

questions.q: What are the four lifecycle states a hosted Claude model moves through, per Anthropic's own documentation?
options: Active, Legacy, Deprecated, Retired
New, Used, Broken, Fixed
Beta, Release, Patch, End-of-life
Free, Paid, Premium, Enterprise
questions.explain: Anthropic's documentation defines the lifecycle as Active (fully supported), Legacy (still works, no updates), Deprecated (not recommended, replacement/date assigned), and Retired (requests fail).

questions.q: As verified in this lesson, which model is described as Anthropic's flagship reasoning tier, open to all customers, as of October 2026?
options: Claude Haiku 4.5
Claude Fable 5.1
Claude Sonnet 5.5
Claude 3 Opus
questions.explain: Claude Fable 5.1 is described directly in Anthropic's own documentation as its most capable model open to all customers, built for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work.

questions.q: Which four criteria does this lesson say to weigh before picking a model?
options: Capabilities, speed, cost, and effort
Color scheme, font, logo, and branding
Country of origin, release date, popularity, and price only
Number of parameters only
questions.explain: Capabilities, speed, cost, and the effort/tuning parameter are the four criteria drawn directly from Anthropic's own 'choosing a model' documentation.

questions.q: Which license did this lesson verify for DeepSeek V4?
options: A fully proprietary, closed license
No license at all
MIT license
A government-restricted license
questions.explain: DeepSeek V4's Flash and Pro checkpoints are MIT-licensed, one of the more permissive open-weight licenses available.

questions.q: In the Messages API, how is conversation history maintained across turns?
options: Anthropic stores the conversation server-side under a session ID
The client resends the full messages array on every call; there is no server-side session
Only the latest message needs to be sent each time
History is stored automatically in the system field
questions.explain: There's no session concept in the Messages API — your application owns and resends the full conversation history on every request.

questions.q: What three fields define a tool in the tools array?
options: endpoint, method, headers
role, content, id
name, description, input_schema
model, max_tokens, messages
questions.explain: A tool definition is its name, a description the model uses to decide when to call it, and a JSON Schema (input_schema) for its arguments.

questions.q: What does stop_reason: "refusal" indicate in a structured-output response?
options: The request succeeded and is ready to parse
The model declined to produce output matching the schema
The connection was dropped mid-stream
The schema itself was invalid JSON
questions.explain: refusal specifically means the model declined to generate schema-conforming output, distinct from end_turn (success) or max_tokens (cut off).

questions.q: How does OpenAI's Chat Completions API wrap its reply, compared to Anthropic's response?
options: Inside a choices array, rather than a top-level content field
Exactly the same way, field for field
As a plain string with no structure
Inside a tools array
questions.explain: OpenAI's response nests the reply as choices[0].message.content; Anthropic returns content directly on the response object.

questions.q: What format is a fine-tuning training file, with one example conversation per line?
options: CSV
JSONL
YAML
Plain unstructured text
questions.explain: JSONL (one JSON object per line) is the standard shape — each line is a full {"messages": [...]} example.

questions.q: What is a held-out evaluation set?
options: The same data used for training, reused for evaluation
A random sample generated by the model itself
The system prompt used during fine-tuning
Labeled examples never used during training, reserved purely for evaluation
questions.explain: Keeping eval data completely separate from training data is what makes the evaluation measure generalization rather than memorization.

questions.q: What does the rank (r) hyperparameter control in LoRA?
options: The number of training examples required
How many epochs training runs for
The base model's context window size
The size of the bottleneck dimension — capacity to learn vs. parameter efficiency
questions.explain: A higher rank gives the adapter more capacity to learn, at the cost of more parameters and less of LoRA's efficiency advantage.

questions.q: What is true about inference cost for a typical fine-tuned model compared to its base model?
options: It is usually identical to the base model's rate
It is usually cheaper, since the model is more specialized
It is usually more expensive per call than the base model — a surcharge, not a discount
Fine-tuned models cannot be queried at inference time at all
questions.explain: Fine-tuned inference commonly carries a per-token surcharge over the base model's rate — a cost that compounds with call volume.

questions.q: What is the key difference between text-to-speech (TTS) and native speech-to-speech?
options: They are two names for the exact same capability
TTS only works in English, while speech-to-speech works in any language
Native speech-to-speech always requires a human in the loop
TTS converts text into audio; native speech-to-speech goes audio in, audio out, without a required text transcript step
questions.explain: TTS still starts from text. Native speech-to-speech skips the required text intermediate step entirely, which is what makes real-time voice agents possible.

questions.q: What does Anthropic's own documentation say about Claude and images?
options: Claude can both understand and generate images
Claude is an image understanding model only — it cannot generate, produce, edit, or create images
Claude can generate images but not read them
Claude has no image capability of any kind
questions.explain: Anthropic documents Claude as image understanding only; image generation is a separate capability Claude does not have.

questions.q: How does this lesson extend Lesson 11's cost/latency/quality framework?
options: It replaces that framework with a completely different one for multimodal tasks
It applies the same cost/latency/quality trade-off thinking to the choice of modality, not just the choice of model
It argues cost and latency no longer matter once multimodal models exist
It claims multimodal calls are always cheaper than text-only calls
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly reuses Lesson 11's framework: text-only is cheapest/fastest, multimodal costs more but can do tasks text-only simply cannot — the same trade-off logic, applied to modality.

questions.q: What is a vision-language model, more precisely than 'a model that can see'?
options: A text model paired with a separate image-classification plugin
A single model trained so images and text share the same underlying reasoning space
A model that can only caption images, never reason about them
A model that converts images into text before any reasoning happens
questions.explain: A VLM is one model trained jointly over images and text, not a text model bolted to a separate image tool — that's why it can reason about a chart, not just describe it.

questions.q: In the SDK's streaming pattern, what does iterating over stream.text_stream give you?
options: The complete raw SSE event objects, including message_start and message_stop
Each text fragment as it arrives, without needing to parse raw SSE events yourself
The token usage counts for the request
A single string containing the entire reply, available only after the stream ends
questions.explain: stream.text_stream is the SDK's higher-level wrapper — it yields each text fragment as it streams in, handling the content_block_delta parsing from Lesson 16 under the hood.

questions.q: Where does this course sit within the AI Engineer career path, per this lesson?
options: It is course 5 of 12 in the Job-Ready stage, with more courses still ahead
It is the very first course in the path
It is the final course in the path, with nothing left afterward
It is not part of any structured career path
questions.explain: Generative AI & LLMs is course 5 of 12 in the AI Engineer path's Job-Ready stage — it's a major milestone, not the end of the path.

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the four rubric requirements for the finished capstone build?
options: It must support image generation
It must be written in a language other than Python
It must avoid using any system prompt
It must use stream: true so replies print incrementally rather than all at once
questions.explain: The four rubric points are: a growing message history, streamed replies (stream: true), a defined system prompt/persona, and a clean way to exit — streaming is explicitly required.
